name: Antonín Slavíček
teaser: The Czech Impressionist of Prague and the countryside — his views of the Vltava, the Vyšehrad, and Bohemian villages glow with a wet, vivid light. He shot himself at 40 after his arm was paralyzed; his student Nechleba finished his final canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: The Vltava scenes or the village landscapes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water and the weather: Slavíček painted rain, wind, and river light with an almost French freedom. His views of Prague from Vyšehrad are full of mist and movement. He said a painter must work 'like a musician, in the open air' — and he did, until his arm failed.

name: Max Švabinský
teaser: The Czech symbolist and painter of monumental allegories — his František Bílek portrait and the Spinning Girl series mix Czech folk motifs with dreamlike grandeur. He was also a superb graphic artist whose stamps and banknotes defined the new state.

exploreAction.targetName: The Spinning Girl or the portrait of František Bílek
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the portrait of the sculptor Bílek: a gaunt, intense figure against a swirl of autumn trees — the Symbolist portrait at its peak. Then his Spinning Girl, where a Czech peasant girl becomes a classical ideal. Švabinský could do national myth and private vision in the same canvas.

name: Jakub Schikaneder
teaser: The Czech painter of dusk and grief — his paintings of lonely women, winter streets, and hospitals are bathed in a melancholy golden gloom. He was fascinated by twilight, and he painted it better than almost anyone.

exploreAction.targetName: Murder in the House or the twilight scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light: Schikaneder's world is lit by lamps, candles, and dying suns — everything is gold and shadow. His famous Murder in the House shows a body on a stairway lit through a doorway, the horror in the stillness. He painted grief with love.

name: Jan Preisler
teaser: The Czech symbolist of fairytale melancholy — his dreamy, autumnal scenes of girls, deer, and longing are painted with a misty lyricism. He said he painted 'the longing of things' — and you can feel it in every canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: The Black Lake or the fairytale scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mood: a girl by a dark lake, a stag in an autumn forest, a fairytale without a story. Preisler's colors are hushed — greys, ochres, greens — and his figures are always slightly lost. He painted the Czech soul as a daydream, and the daydream is beautiful.

name: Josef Čapek
teaser: The Czech painter who named the robot — he coined 'robot' for his brother Karel's play — and painted Cubist still lifes and vivid street scenes. He died in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945, days before liberation.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cubist still lifes or the paintings of the city
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Čapek builds a still life: fruit, bottles, and cloth cut into facets, like Czech Cubist architecture. Then his later, freer paintings of streets and figures — brighter, more human. He wrote a book about dogs while imprisoned, and painted when he could. A gentle man in a brutal time.

name: Emil Filla
teaser: The leader of Czech Cubism — his fractured landscapes, still lifes, and 'fight' paintings brought Picasso and Braque's revolution to Prague. He spent the war in a concentration camp, survived, and returned to paint again.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cubist still lifes or the Reader of Dostoevsky
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Filla fractures a table and its fruit into facets — Cubism with a Slavic weight. His Reader of Dostoevsky turns a man with a book into a monument of angled planes. He wrote art theory, fought in the Legion, and survived the camps. A life as fractured and whole as his paintings.

name: Bohumil Kubišta
teaser: The Czech painter who fused Cubism with raw color — his factories, saints, and city squares are built from faceted planes in brutal, singing hues. He died of flu in 1918 at 34, leaving a career that predicted half of 20th-century Czech art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Kiss of Death or the factory scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Kiss of Death: a skeleton embraces a man in a field of faceted blue — death as geometry. Then his factories: chimneys, roofs, and sky cut into planes of red, blue, and ochre. Kubišta brought order and violence together; the war killed him before his promise matured.

name: Václav Špála
teaser: The Czech painter of blue — he painted the Vltava, Czech villages, and sunflowers in a personal, luminous blue that made him the most beloved Czech painter of the century. His color sings, even when the subject is snow.

exploreAction.targetName: The Vltava scenes or the sunflower paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the blue: Špála's rivers, hills, and skies all run toward cobalt — he said blue was 'the color of Czech freedom.' His paintings are full of sun and water and a stubborn joy. He painted his country the way a composer writes an anthem.

name: František Muzika
teaser: The Czech painter of dream landscapes — he moved from Czech Cubism to dreamlike scenes of memory and interior rooms, and finally to abstract visions of cosmic order. He also designed avant-garde theater sets for Osvobozené divadlo.

exploreAction.targetName: The dream interiors or the late abstract works
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the dream rooms: staircases, windows, and shadows arranged like memories of a house you once lived in. Then his late abstractions — circles, discs, and floating forms, calmer and more cosmic. Muzika crossed every style of his century and made each one his own.

name: Toyen
teaser: The Czech Surrealist who refused gender labels — Marie Čermínová, who painted as 'Toyen' — created landscapes of desire, absence, and revolution with a cool, precise technique. She escaped Prague and died in Paris, one of Surrealism's most original voices.

exploreAction.targetName: The Revolver in the Hand or the dream landscapes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Toyen's world: empty rooms, cold landscapes, objects floating without context — desire rendered as architecture. Her paintings from the Nazi occupation are full of hidden defiance. She said her art was 'a declaration of the right to dream.' The dreams are strange and unforgettable.

name: Jindřich Štyrský
teaser: The Czech Surrealist of dark collages and poetic photographs — his Artificialist paintings with Toyen and his dreamlike photographs of Prague are among the most unsettling works of Czech modernism. He died young of a heart condition, aged 43.

exploreAction.targetName: The Artificialist paintings or the photograph albums
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Artificialist canvases: blurs, veils, and drifting forms that feel like the retina after a dream. Then his photographs — lonely streets, shop windows, shadowy corners of Prague, shot like crime scenes of the unconscious. Štyrský saw the city as a dreamer sees it.

name: Josef Šíma
teaser: The Czech-French painter of cosmic landscapes — his visions of deserts, planets, and inner horizons are painted with a quiet, spiritual precision. He was a founder of the Czech group Devětsil and spent most of his life in Paris.

exploreAction.targetName: The inner landscapes or the cosmic visions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the horizons: Šíma painted vast, empty landscapes — a plain, a planet, a threshold — that feel like places inside the mind. His color is muted and his geometry is exact. He said he painted 'the image of a world beyond the visible.' Stand long enough and you almost see it.

name: Zdeněk Sklenář
teaser: The Czech painter of calligraphic dreams — his paintings blend pre-Columbian imagery, Chinese calligraphy, and Czech modernism into webs of line and color. He was a devoted traveler who turned the world's scripts into his private writing.

exploreAction.targetName: The calligraphic compositions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lines: Sklenář's paintings are full of signs that almost mean something — birds, glyphs, characters from lost alphabets. He collected scripts the way others collect stamps, then let them dance on his canvases. A painter of writing that never quite resolves into words.

name: Mikuláš Medek
teaser: The Czech painter of the absurd and the totalitarian — his paintings mix private mythology with political dread, from his early surrealist dreams to his late, sardonic 'dipteras' (flies). He spent years silenced by the regime, then became a legend.

exploreAction.targetName: The early surreal works or the late diptera series
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the diptera series: huge flies, painted with loving, grotesque detail — a pun on 'fly' and a metaphor for surveillance. Medek painted under totalitarianism and developed a private language of symbols to survive it. His colors are acidic, his mood is defiant, and his flies are unforgettable.

name: Jiří Kolář
teaser: The Czech poet-artist who invented the collage-chiasm — he cut up poems, pictures, and pages and wove them into new texts and images. His 'confrontations' and 'rollages' are among the most inventive art of the postwar era.

exploreAction.targetName: The collage-poems or the rollages
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a chiasm: a poem cut into strips and woven vertically into another poem — two texts braided into a third. Then his rollages, where images are sliced and reassembled like fabric. Kolář began as a poet, and he never stopped being one — he just changed the material.

name: Karel Teige
teaser: The Czech theorist and collage artist of Poetism and Devětsil — his typographic and photomontage works are among the most beautiful of the Czech avant-garde. He declared 'art for all the senses' and meant it.

exploreAction.targetName: The typographic works or the photomontages
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Teige arranges type, photos, and shapes: a page becomes a composition, a collage becomes a manifesto. He was the engine of the Czech avant-garde — editor, organizer, provocateur. His collages of women and machines are surrealist poetry made of scissors and paste.

name: Adriaen van Ostade
teaser: The Dutch genre painter of peasant interiors — his smoky taverns, backyards, and schoolrooms are full of laughing, fighting, drinking figures painted with warmth and detail. He was Rembrandt's contemporary and the best chronicler of Dutch village life.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peasants' Tavern or the interior scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light through the window: a smoky room, a fiddle, a brawl, and faces lit from one side. Van Ostade painted the same peasants all his life, in every mood — and they're never sentimental, just alive. Rembrandt owned several of his paintings, which is the best review he could get.

name: Jan Steen
teaser: The Dutch painter of chaos — his household scenes are full of spilled wine, laughing children, smoking grandmothers, and moral messages hidden in the mess. The Dutch still say 'a Jan Steen household' to mean a happy disorder.

exploreAction.targetName: The Feast of Saint Nicholas or the disorderly household
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Feast of Saint Nicholas: a family erupts with joy — one child cries, another celebrates, grandmother grins. Every detail is a clue: the shoe, the gingerbread, the birch rod hidden in the corner. Steen painted chaos with a moralist's agenda and a comedian's heart.

name: Gerard ter Borch
teaser: The Dutch master of the quiet conversation — his small paintings of elegant interiors, with their silken gowns and hushed exchanges, are the most refined genre scenes of the Dutch Golden Age. The lace and satin in his paintings are still unmatched.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gallant Conversation or the portraits
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fabric: ter Borch painted the white satin of a woman's gown so it catches the light like real silk — no Dutch painter did it better. His scenes are full of glances and gestures that mean more than words. A whole society's manners, captured in a room.

name: Gabriel Metsu
teaser: The Dutch painter of domestic harmony — his kitchen scenes, letter readers, and sickbed visits are painted with Vermeer-like light and a warmth all his own. He died at 38, at the height of his powers.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sick Child or the kitchen scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Sick Child: a mother holds her feverish daughter while light falls through the window — tenderness painted with total attention. Metsu's interiors glow with the same calm as Vermeer's, but his people are always doing something: cooking, reading, caring. Life, painted lovingly.

name: Pieter de Hooch
teaser: The Dutch painter of courtyards and light — his views through doorways into sunlit yards are masterpieces of perspective and atmosphere, nearly equal to Vermeer. He painted the Dutch home as a place of order, light, and peace.

exploreAction.targetName: The Courtyard of a House in Delft (National Gallery, London) — the geometry
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the doorways: de Hooch framed one room through another, leading your eye out to the sunlit yard — an architecture of light. A woman sweeps, a child plays, bricks glow warm. He and Vermeer shared the same Delft, the same light, and the same love of the ordinary made sacred.
